The verse's first sentence is not yet a threat but a fact about visibility, and its placement matters: abuse of signs is exactly the kind of deed that flourishes in the expectation of no audience — private sneers, edited readings, the organized heckling of recitations, all of it conducted by people who believed the venue was theirs. "They are not hidden from Us" is therefore a sentence with the quiet menace of a police blotter: the first-person plural belongs to the One the verses are about, so the offense is aimed at the One who is watching. The chapter has spent twenty verses proving that nothing is hidden — the organs keep what the owners deny (41:20), the Record holds the atom's weight (the Book's standing rule, 34:3) — and this verse adds only the corollary: the abuse of revelation, being an act in the world, is in the record like any other, and the "We" who are not outpaced is the same "We" who apportioned the earth's sustenance (41:10) and will cast the Fire's residents into it. No new machinery; just the application of the sūrah's whole physics of witnessing to its own attackers.

**The Question That Is a Court Session**

"Who is better: the one cast into the Fire, or the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?" — an interrogative of the sūrah's family: comparison posed as a question to force the only possible answer, asked here between two figures the audience itself has just watched described, the condemned assembly of verses nineteen through twenty-four and the steadfast of thirty through thirty-two. The commentators report the old tries to pin the two men to individuals — Abū Jahl and the Prophet, or some pair of enemies and martyrs — and the same readers record the sounder judgment (IJ, Ṭs): the phrasing is a general comparison with representative instances, which is what makes the verse a court rather than an anecdote; any hearer can occupy either dock, and the sūrah intends at least one of them to. The question also keeps the chapter's favorite logic of the self-evident: "better" is not defined here, because the sūrah has spent its whole creation sequence establishing the scale by which everything — security, sustenance, reward — is measured, and the two positions on either side of it need no elaboration from a text that calls itself explained (41:3).

**"Do What You Will" — the Echo of Defiance Returned**

The imperative clause is the verse's most terrible sentence precisely because it is an old quotation. The sūrah's own opening had recorded the defiant declaration — "So do whatever you want and so shall we" (41:5) — the leaders' settlement of coexistence with the messenger, and now the chapter replies with the same idiom in God's mouth: do as you will (41:40). Between the two sentences the sūrah has built its whole argument, and the reply's force is the absence of any restriction: the free permission, the respite in which the will runs its full course, is exactly what the record and the comparison then weigh. The old exegetes mark the clause as a threat of abandonment — the most severe form of divine address, the withdrawal of correction — and the echo proves the sūrah's artistry: the audience's own words are returned to them after the entire cosmos has testified, the way a court returns a defendant's earlier statement when the verdict is ready, and the two occurrences of "do" are the chapter's way of measuring the distance between arrogance's permission and the permission that ends in the Fire.

**"All-Seeing of What You Do" — the Sense Assigned to the End**

The closing clause names the attribute in the sense of sight, and the sūrah's audience had been hearing sight talked about since the boast of the not-seeing tribe (41:15's "Did they not see?"), so the verse ends not with a new doctrine but with the chapter's recurring verdict on the faculty: the seeing that fails a human being is unavailable here. The translators' small compound "All-Seeing of what you do" carries the participle of constant perception — not "will see" but "is seeing," tense without gap — and the grammar is why the "do what you will" before it is not nihilism but its opposite: what you do is, at the moment of doing, already seen, already mine, already in the record. The verse's movement is thus the whole chapter's epistemology in four beats: the abuse (an act), the not-hidden (a fact), the comparison (a verdict), and the seeing (the tense of it all). A sign that ends in the verb of vision, in a sūrah about a Book that demanded only ears and a heart, closes the circle the chapter's opening sequence began — and the two verses that follow will return to the Reminder the abusers had been slanting, to say whose Book it is.

Structurally the verse is the sūrah's midpoint in miniature: it summarizes the first forty verses in one sentence — the Book (3–6), the creation-argument (9–12), the destructions (13–18), the testimony (19–24), the ethics (33–38), the signs (37, 39) — and turns the chapter toward the Reminder's final defense (41:41–44).
verses.41:
> Indeed, those who deny the Reminder after it has come to them ˹are doomed˺, for it is truly a mighty Book

**A Sentence with Its Verdict Elided**

The verse's first clause names the deniers and then, in Arabic, stops: the consequence is left unspoken, and the next clause — "for it is truly a mighty Book" — begins as though the first had already finished. The commentators supply what is missing, with real disagreement: they will be punished (Q), they are stubborn and obstinate (Bḍ), they are recompensed for their disbelief (IJ); others read the opening verb as itself an asseveration with "deny" doubled, or let the sentence complete at the end of verse forty-four — "they are being called from a faraway place." The variety is honest exegesis of an ellipsis: the Arabic leaves a hanging threat, and a hanging threat is the point. The sūrah declines to write the punishment into this verse because the next two clauses will write the dignity of what was denied, and the contrast — no verdict stated, all majesty stated — is the verse's own form of the verdict. Readers who demand the elision be resolved should prefer those who read it as deliberate suspense: the sentence is a raised sword held in the air of the chapter.

**"The Reminder" — the Book's Name for Itself**

* adh-Dhikr* — the Reminder — and the name is theology in miniature. The root *dh-k-r* carries both mention and mindfulness, and a *dhikr* is a thing that puts the mind back in contact with what it already knew: not information but recollection. The sūrah's own usage proves the register: the Quran is "a blessed reminder which We have revealed" (21:50), and the chapter has built its opening on exactly this premise — a Book of explained verses "for people who know" (41:3), addressed to a faculty already stocked by creation and conscience. The name then indicts the denial with its own mechanism: those who refuse a Reminder do not lack news, they refuse to remember, which is the sūrah's whole diagnosis since verse four's turning-away. The title is also why the English "deny the Reminder" outperforms "disbelieve the Book" here: the crime against a reminder is dismissal, not doubt, and dismissal requires no evidence to be wrongful — only attention to be avoided. The verse's temporal clause — when it comes to them — converts denial from a condition into a course, and the Book elsewhere describes the same conversion in the People of the Book: "when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had in their hands, they rejected it" (2:89), recognition first, rejection after, and the sequence named as the atrocity.

**Why Noise Cannot Answer a Mighty Book**

The chapter has already told what Mecca intended to do about the recitation — drown it out (41:26) — and verse forty-one's claim answers that policy in the order of argument: a policy of acoustics is aimed at a book whose quality is *izza*, might, and might is precisely what noise cannot reach. The sūrah's earlier verses made the same point cosmically: the lowest heaven is ringed with lamps as a guard (41:12), and the Reminder's protection is of that order; the exegetes read "mighty" here as the Quran's share in the guarding of the transmission — what the soothsayers cannot steal, the hecklers cannot mute, and the deniers cannot date earlier than it is. The claim is testable in the chapter's own terms: the Book that opened as a descent from the Merciful (41:2) has been standing, verse by verse, in front of an audience that has tried everything except refutation — silence, noise, mockery, distortion (41:40) — and every attempt is, in this verse's ledger, an incident in the Book's history, not an amendment to its text. Might is the name for what survives its management.

The chapter's long middle had argued the sender through earth, heaven, and the destroyed; now it argues the message, in the same order the opening sequence set (descent, exposition, function, refusal, 41:2–6), and the reader arrives where the sūrah began with thirty-eight verses of proof laid behind the claims.
verses.42:
> It cannot be proven false from any angle. ˹It is˺ a revelation from the ˹One Who is˺ All-Wise, Praiseworthy

**The Spatial Idiom of an Unassailable Claim**

*Lā yaʾtīhi-l-bāṭilu min bayni yadayhi wa-lā min khalfihī* — falsehood does not come upon it, from between its hands or from behind it — and the idiom is architectural: in Arabic speech a building with no approach from in front or behind has no side left for siege. The translators' "from any angle" captures the sense, and the sūrah's own earlier vocabulary explains the choice: this is the same language of guarded access with which the chapter described the heaven ringed with lamps against eavesdroppers (41:12, and "We protected it from every accursed devil" — 15:17), so the Book's immunity belongs to the same security system as the sky's. Falsehood is personified as a would-be visitor, and the sentence rules that the visitor is barred at both the door and the rear gate. The claim is concrete because the attack it denies is concrete: the chapter has just recorded distortion (41:40), noise (41:26), and denial after arrival (41:41), and answers all three with a single architectural no.

**The Test the Book Invites Instead of Banning**

A book that cannot be reached by falsehood could simply demand faith; this one issues a falsification challenge: "Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies" (4:82), and the same self-description opens the people-of-the-cave chapter, "All praise is for Allah Who has revealed the Book to His servant, allowing no crookedness in it" (18:1) — crookedness, *ʿiwaj*, the bent in a wall or a road, being the very defect the present verse's architecture denies. The pairing is instructive: incorruptibility in the Quran is not asserted against examination but as the result of one, and "no crookedness" and "no falsehood from any angle" are the negative and positive faces of a single, checkable claim — that a document of this size, this age, this many uses, contains no self-refutation and has admitted none. The sūrah's audience — a market of poets, genealogists, and contract-lawyers — understood the value of a clean record, and the verse is written for people who audit.

**Preserved Above, Guarded Below**

The verse's claim stands on a support the Book states elsewhere: "In a glorious Quran, inscribed on a Preserved Tablet" (85:21–22), and the promise of the Guardian — "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" (15:9) — is why the two directions of attack fail from only one source. The chain of preservation runs from a tablet that is kept to a text that keeps: the lower book's untouchability is the upper's custody, reported, and the sūrah's own transmission has been under the security of the lamps since the first night (41:12). What the commentators draw from the structure is a modest doctrine: the Book does not guard itself, and piety toward it is not directed to the parchment but to the Faithful that holds it — which is also why "mighty" (41:41) and "cannot be approached by falsehood" (42) are one claim twice: might, here, means the borrowed kind, the inviolability of what God has decided to keep. The verse, read with its sources, is a statement of custody, not of magic.

**Why These Two Verses Sit Where They Do**

Forty-one and forty-two are the chapter's constitutional pair — might and immunity — and their placement is the sūrah's last argumentative act before it turns to the messenger's consolation (41:43) and the defense of the Arabic (41:44). The Book itself, in the middle of the chapter's end, receives two verses of status — and the sequence says something exact about the sūrah's mind: a messenger's message is his person in court, and Mecca's case against the man (41:5) had become its case against the Book (41:26, 41:40), so the chapter answers for both at once, vindicating the Reminder in the same breath in which it will vindicate its bearer: nothing is said to you except what was said before (41:43).

The root of *maḥīd* is the root of *al-ḥamdu*, the praise that opens the Book (1:2), and the sūrah ends its scripture-brief on that echo: what returns to the Praiseworthy from every angle is the recitation of praise itself, and the Prophet's own "station of praise" (17:79) is the human counterpart to the divine epithet.
verses.43:
> ˹O Prophet!˺ Nothing is said to you ˹by the deniers˺ except what was already said to the messengers before you. Surely your Lord is ˹the Lord˺ of forgiveness and painful punishment

**The Shortest Consolation in the Book**

The verse's grammar is an exclusion — *mā qawlu illā...* — and its content is a list the Prophet never has to compile because God compiles it for him: nothing is said to you except what was already said to the messengers before you. The technique of prophetic consolation in this Book rarely rises above this brevity, and it never falls below it: the wound of insult is treated not by denial ("they do not really mean it") nor by compensation ("they will be punished"), but by inclusion — the abuse is catalogued as standard equipment of the office. The Cattle chapter says the same from the other side: "It is not your honesty they question—it is Allah's signs that the wrongdoers deny" (6:33). Once the insult is known to be part of the job description rather than a verdict on the man, its power to isolate dies, and the sūrah's one sentence does that work for the whole chapter: the audience that hurled it is being described, not obeyed. The passive verb leaves the sayers anonymous — "nothing is said to you" — and the anonymity is forensic, because the chapter has already put the sayings on the record without naming speakers: the resolution to drown the recitation (41:26), the hearts-under-coverings excuse (41:5), the demand for an angel or a different Quran.

**"The Messengers Before You" — the Sūrah's Precedent Chain**

The verse's genitive plural does real historical work. The chapter has already run its own precedent list — ʿĀd and Thamūd thunderbolted (41:13–18), the associates appointed over those drowning out the recitation (41:25–26), Pharaoh's drowning in the Book's telling (10:90) — and it will cite Moses' disputed scripture immediately after this verse (41:45), so "the messengers before you" is not a general comfort but the sūrah's own bibliography. The Sandhills chapter's formula pairs the same endurance with its precedent: "So endure patiently, as did the Messengers of Firm Resolve" (46:35), and the Cattle chapter states the office's law entire: messengers before him were rejected, but patiently endured the rejection and the persecution until help came (6:34). The source-note on this verse makes the connection by word rather than verse: what Mecca says now — sorcerer, poet, mad — is what the "possessors of resolve" heard; the consolation is that the man who hears it stands in a column of men who heard it and were vindicated, and the column, not the insult, is the historical fact.

**The Painful Punishment Named in Front of the Comforter**

It deserves remark that the punishment clause is addressed to the messenger, not to the enemies — *your Lord* is the Lord of both — and the choice keeps the sūrah's ethics intact: the prophet is not promised vengeance as his portion. Severe punishment is stated as an attribute of God's governance, not as the servant's entitlement, and the man being consoled receives the whole picture in the same sentence so that his patience is not built on hope alone. The chapter's vocabulary already made this distinction: the lost were "made to taste" humiliation (41:16) and the promised mercy is likewise "tasted" (41:50's verb, in its own way); punishment belongs to God's report about the world, not to the wounded's wish list. A consolation that must include the pain of the other party's fate on the horizon is the Book's way of preventing consolation from curdling into resentment's relief — the Prophet is healed of the insult precisely by not being handed the punisher's role.
verses.44:
> Had We revealed it as a non-Arabic Quran, they would have certainly argued, “If only its verses were made clear ˹in our language˺. What! A non-Arabic revelation for an Arab audience!” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “It is a guide and a healing to the believers. As for those who disbelieve, there is deafness in their ears and blindness to it ˹in their hearts˺. It is as if they are being called from a faraway place.”

**"An Arab Reciter and a Foreign Book" — the Complaint in One Line**

The translators render the objectors' exclamation — "What! A non-Arabic revelation for an Arab audience!" — and the note in this chapter's sources records the classical parsing: the construction is one of astonishment, treating the mismatch of vessel and content as inconceivable, exactly as they had objected to a human messenger at all (the same astonishment the Book quotes from them: "Is this not merely a human like yourselves?" — 21:3). The astonishment is the point the sūrah exposes: the objectors are not asking for a clearer book, they are asserting that a clear book could not look like this — and the chapter's own title-word answers in its own tongue: verses that are *fuṣṣilat*, detailed, explained (41:3), a claim the objectors' quoted demand ("If only its verses were detailed") repeats verbatim in its root while pretending the book never made it. The irony is exact: they demand the very verb that names the sūrah, from a text that opens by saying the verb has been done.

**The Language as Mercy, Not Accident**

Elsewhere the Book states the rule behind this verse's choice: "We have sent no messenger except in the language of his people, so that he may make it clear for them" (14:4), and the making-it-clear of that verse is the same root-family as the detail here — the Arabic of the Quran is not an ethnic privilege but a compliance with the logic of guidance, which is intelligibility to the first audience. The Ornaments chapter adds the matching half: "Certainly, We have made it a Quran in Arabic so perhaps you will understand" (43:3), a verb of making that, like 41:44's counterfactual, presents the tongue as deliberately selected for a cognitive end. When the sūrah's hearers argued that an Arab book proves nothing about its source, this verse's reply is that the opposite book would have proved nothing too — the objection tracks the audience's disposition, not the evidence — and the choice of Arabic is simply God's mercy being literal, speaking to people the way they actually hear.

**"A Guide and a Healing" — the Two Offices**

The commanded announcement gives the book two functions before it gives the enemies any: *hudā* and *shifāʾ* — direction for where to go, medicine for what is wrong. The pairing occurs in the same order in Jonah: "there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers" (10:57), and in the Night Journey chapter, which adds the side-effect on the proud: "We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss" (17:82). The source-note here runs both: guidance for the outward road, healing for the inward sickness, and readers of this sūrah will recall that its Meccan opponents diagnosed the book as the disease (a bewitchment, a nuisance to be drowned, 41:26), while the verse proposes the opposite anatomy — the book is what treats the condition that made them object. Guide and healing are then one mercy with two addresses: the road and the patient.

**"Deafness in Their Ears and Blindness to It"**

The verse's diagnosis completes an anatomy the sūrah has been charting since its early denials: hearts "under coverings" from what the messenger invites (41:5), and now a weight in the ears and blindness in what the translators mark, by bracket, as the hearts — three organs, three refusals, one condition: the senses are functioning but closed on the object. This is the same sūrah that made organs testify against their owners (41:20) and gave the skin the final line (41:21); here, before the trial, it records the disability voluntarily, a deafness that arrives every time the ear is paid to drown a reciter (41:26) — noise practiced until it becomes an organ.
verses.45:
> Indeed, We had given Moses the Scripture, but differences arose regarding it. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺. They are truly in alarming doubt about it

**The Scripture That Got Moses No Peace**

The verse takes the chapter's own book-objection and hands it to Moses: the Scripture was given, and *they disputed it* — the same verb pair the chapter's audience was enacting. The move completes the sequence that began with consolation (41:43) and ran through the language defense (41:44): Mecca's quarrel with the Reminder is not a flaw in the Reminder but the standard fate of revealed books, and the sūrah's evidence for that claim is the book whose law Mecca's own pilgrims half-respected. The classical readers note the past-tense structure does the whole argumentative work: *ātaynā Mūsā al-kitāba fa-ikhtalifa fīh* — giving followed immediately by disagreement — no interval, no golden age; the Scripture arrives and the dispute arrives with it, so the dispute cannot be treated as evidence against the Scripture. The doubt that gnaws at a messenger hearing "why not an angel?" finds, in this verse's file, a colleague's identical case, settled by a prior decree that the messenger's own Lord has already issued.

**"Had It Not Been for a Prior Decree" — The Law of Delayed Verdicts**

The conditional clause is the sūrah's theodicy in one formula: the reason the Meccans are still walking is not that the book is untested but that a decree has gone before, deferring judgment to the appointed day — exactly the wording of Hūd, whose Moses-verse is this one's twin: "Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled at once" (11:110), and again in Jonah's, with the identical decree-clause: "Humanity was once nothing but a single community ˹of believers˺, but then they differed. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺" (10:19). The sūrah has been describing the same machinery since verse thirteen — a thunderbolt-warning deferred until the appointed associates finish their beautifying, when "the fate of earlier communities of jinn and humans has been justified against them" (41:25); here the grammar makes that sequence general law. The respite is not indifference; it is the space in which the book can be loved, and the sūrah says, in practice: the dispute is not unjudged, it is on schedule.

**"Distressing Doubt" — the Doubt That Has a Class**

The final clause diagnoses the disputers: *fahum fī shakkin minhu mūrij* — and the adjective's root means to agitate, to churn, the water stirred until nothing at the bottom stays visible. The word-choice marks the doubt this sūrah cares about: not the honest perplexity of a seeker (which the book's healing answers) but the churned state of people who have made dispute their position — doubt as identity, which the translation's "distressing" catches in its English double sense: they are in doubt, and the doubt is what distresses them. The source-note compares the Quran's own counter-claim at its opening — "a book about which there is no doubt, a guide for the mindful" (2:2), the certainty of the text matching the anxiety of the readers who will not submit to it. The sūrah's doubt is never epistemic weather; it is the psychological weather around a verdict already offered, which is why the chapter answers it not with more proof but with anatomy (41:5's coverings, 41:44's deafness) and precedent (this verse's Moses).

**The Verse's Place in the Chapter's Court**

Read as procedure, verses forty-one through forty-five are the closing brief on the Book, and this verse is its precedent-and-punishment argument: might and immunity asserted (41:41–42), the bearer consoled and the language defended (41:43–44), and now the court's final exhibit — the same trial run before, with the same charges, and with judgment lawfully deferred. The structure is why the verse cannot be cut without collapsing the chapter: the Meccan objections were "why not a book of another kind?" and "why not our tongue?" and "this is an old forgery" — the verse concedes the third by generalizing it into history (yes, like Moses' book; the objection is ancestral), which is the strongest reply available: an objection that has been refuted once in every scripture has lost its novelty even where it has not lost its volume. The court closes its case file on the Book with the observation that the defendants have brought a rehearsed complaint, and the prior decree keeps the sentence open.

The chapter has shown the terminus of the alternative once — the drowning man's faith arriving as verdict, not rescue (10:90–91), because his case had been cut; the deferral of Mecca's *quḍāʾ* is the difference between a sūrah and an epitaph.
verses.46:
> Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss. Your Lord is never unjust to ˹His˺ creation

**No Surplus to God, No Shortfall**

The clause's theology is the negative the chapter has been proving through forty-five verses: creation's worship adds nothing to the Lord's treasury and its rebellion nothing to His loss, so all accounting is for the creature. The Spider chapter puts it exactly in these terms — "Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss. Then to your Lord you will all be returned" (45:15) — and Jonah states the bare rule beneath it: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves" (10:44). The difference from this verse is the object of the closing: there "people," here "creation" (*khalq*), and the widening is not stylistic: the God addressed as Lord of the creation (41:9's *fāṭir* passage) is the God whose non-injustice covers every creature in the smoke-and-order universe the sūrah has described, not merely the covenant class. The verse thus closes the chapter's cosmology and its ethics with one clause each: the Lord of all the created does no wrong to any of it.

**"To Their Own Selves" — the Ledger Without a Third Party**

Readers of this verse in the chapter's own light should note that the sūrah's middle already staged the same doctrine in narrative form: the enemies' assumption that God would not hear the small talk (41:22) was punished as a mistake about accounts, not manners; the organs testifying against the owners (41:20) proved that the deed never leaves the doer's house; the skin's speech (41:21) was the same ownership drama in a single organ. The good "is for yourselves" and the evil "is against yourselves" with the dryness of a contract clause, and the dryness is the verse's rhetoric — after fifty verses of thunder, rain, testimony, and welcome, the settlement is the shortest possible sentence with no image in it, because images were what the dispute argued about, and the ownership of deeds is not figurative.

**The Verse Against Victimhood and Against Bargaining**

The double clause disciplines the two ways a religious audience can misread its own fate. If the believer's good is "for themselves," piety is not a favor done to God for which His Book can be dunned for payment — the bargaining spirit that the chapter mocked (41:24's fruitless endurance — "Even if they endure patiently, the Fire will always be their home" — and 39:10's world-priceless Hereafter) is answered here in plain grammar, reward already assigned to its owner. And if the evildoer's evil is "against themselves," the claim of persecution by the message loses its nerve: the loss the hearer risks is not the prophet's malice but their own material, and the sūrah's warnings are then not weapons but signage. The Quran's standing rule of moral physics closes the Cave's record-scene in the same words: "And your Lord will never wrong anyone" (18:49) — the readers quote that clause as this verse's gloss — and its function in the chapter is to leave the audience no court of appeal but God, and no defendant but themselves.

**"Never Unjust to ˹His˺ Creation" — the Name Doing Double Duty**

The final clause's negation is the strongest available in Arabic: *mā anta ʿalayhim bi-ẓallāmin* would be "you are not a tyrant over them"; the verse's *wa-mā rabbuka bi-ẓallāmin li-l-khalq* is a permanent attribute-negation — your Lord is not, at any time, of the class of the unjust toward creation. The possessive "your Lord" does the same work verse forty-three's "your Lord" did — the same Subject of consolation — and the sūrah ties the two together: the God who forgives and punishes (41:43's pair) is the God whose punishment is definitionally not injustice, because justice is what the ownership clause just guaranteed — each soul receiving its own. The note in the sources records the readers saying exactly this, that the verse removes every ground for the complaint that God punishes unfairly: He takes from none what was not theirs to keep and gives to none more than their own. The mercy-first structure of the chapter (names of compassion at its head, forgiveness named before punishment at 41:43) stands uncancelled: severity in this book is not the opposite of the first sentence's mercy but its legal complement.

The chapter's book-brief (41:41–45) ended with parties in "distressing doubt," and verse forty-six steps back from the dispute to the rule that settles every such dispute: deeds are owned — good to the doer's own selves, evil to their own loss.

What follows (41:47–54) turns to the Hour's knowledge, the associates' disappearance, the human's temperament, and the final challenge of the signs, but the moral load-bearing wall is in place: a reader who accepts the ownership clause accepts everything else the chapter said about patience, honesty, and refuge, because each of those teachings is the clause applied to a situation.
verses.47:
> With Him ˹alone˺ is the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit comes out of its husk, nor does a female conceive or deliver without His knowledge. And ˹consider˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are My ˹so-called˺ associate-gods?” They will cry, “We declare before you that none of us testifies to that ˹any longer˺.”

**The Hour's Date in a Locked Drawer**

The chapter's final sequence opens by removing the question Mecca actually kept asking — when is this promise? — with an answer no committee of chronologists can appeal: to Him alone belongs the knowledge of the Hour. Luqmān turns the same lock: "Indeed, Allah alone has the knowledge of the Hour. He sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs" (31:34) — rain, wombs, and the Hour in one breath, which is why botany and obstetrics belong in verses about the doctrine of the Last Day — and the Parties chapter converts the sealed date into a summons: "That knowledge is only with Allah. You never know, perhaps the Hour is near" (33:63). The sequence of the sūrah's own verbs matters too: knowledge is *ʿindahu* — with Him — an idiom of possession, and the chapter's last word about timing is thus not "it is hidden" but "it is owned," which removes the date from the market where the deniers hoped to buy it or debunk it.

**Fruit in the Husk, the Child in the Womb**

The minute clause — no fruit coming out of its sheath, no female conceiving or delivering, except by His knowledge — is the sūrah's answer to the scale of what the Hour's knowledge implies. The Thunder chapter gives the omniscience its inventory: "Allah knows what every female bears and what increases and decreases in the wombs. And with Him everything is determined with precision" (13:8), and the Cattle chapter closes on leaves and seeds: "Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth" (6:59). The Hour's hour is thus not withheld because it is far away; it is withheld because nothing comes to birth in this universe except through that same knowledge, and the distance was always in the questioners, not in the timing (41:44's "faraway place").

**"Where Are My Associate-Gods?"**

The Day's question is one of the Quran's most theatrical: He calls out to them, where are My partners? — and the sūrah's audience had already heard this interrogative at 46:5's "who are those you invoked besides Him?" (the question that opens the next section of this very chapter's family). Its force here is procedural rather than emotional: the court does not ask whether the partners are real but produces them, as a prosecutor produces the exhibit the defense promised, and the silence after the question is the evidence. The phrasing "My associate-gods" (shurakāʾī, the translation's own compound) puts possession on the lips of the accused's own theology for the last time, and the chapter's long argument about partners — the creation sequence that made them unable to create (41:9's "they did not create anything," the same logic) — now arrives at its only possible endpoint: the day names the missing.

**The Last Witness Statement — Nobody Will Testify**

Their reply is the verse's masterpiece, and it is a sentence about testimony: "We declare before you that none of us testifies to that" — the associates, and their worshippers with them, formally withdrawing the evidence. The sūrah has run on witnesses since verse nineteen (the gathered enemies, 41:19), with the organs deposing (41:20) and the skin delivering the closing statement (41:21), and here the chain completes in the reverse direction: the last testimony the court takes is the witnesses' recantation — the gods testifying that they were never gods. The reply is strictly a juridical act, a witness-bearing they now deny ever having offered, and readers should note that the men do not say "we lied" but "none of us testifies" — the register of the courtroom, where the case for partners fails not for falsehood but for want of witnesses, the sūrah's most devastating sentence about the polytheists' entire religion: a claim that cannot find one soul to attest to it, on the day when every soul wants to.
verses.48:
> Whatever ˹idols˺ they used to invoke besides Allah will fail them. And they will realize that they will have no escape

**The Verb of Vanishing**

*Ḍalla ʿanhum* — rendered "will fail them" — is the root of going astray and being lost, the same verb the chapter will choose for the most astray of men (41:52's *aḍallu*), and here it is not the worshippers who are lost but the worshipped. The verse's choice is worth the philology: the idols do not die here, though the Book's plainest description of them was always physical — gods "who cannot create anything but are themselves created. Nor can they protect or benefit themselves" (25:3) — and they do not argue; they go astray from the scene, vanishing from the story at the moment the story needs them. The sūrah has already said everything it will ever say about partners in the negative — they create nothing, they profit nothing, and for the wrongdoers there is "neither a close friend nor intercessor to be heard" (40:18) — and this verb is the sum: failure is not the idols' defeat but their withdrawal from the story at the moment the story needs them. An invocation whose object closes its doors is the chapter's last word on prayer to the unreal.

**"They Used to Invoke" — The Grammar of Habit**

The Arabic puts the idols' whole career in the imperfect of repeated past, *mā kānū yadʿūna* — that which they had kept calling — and the sūrah's audiences hear it as a record of practice, not conviction. The older readers stress that the clause is the verse's real verdict: nothing in it says the men ever believed the stones could save; it says what they did, repeatedly, in the face of every contrary evidence their own lives offered — which is the definition of the religion this chapter has described from the start: not a false theory but a habit sustained against its own data — the private-half assumption, "Allah did not know much of what you used to do" (41:22), and the public noise-policy (41:26) its civic half. When the verse says the invoked will fail, it describes habit meeting its term; the verbs of "invoking" and "failing" differ only in tense, and the whole of idolatry in this sūrah is a present tense that does not know it is past.

**The Oath They Will Still Try**

The source preserves the Day's matching scene from the Cattle chapter, where the same men, facing the same question, attempt one last evidence-based plea: "Their only argument will be: 'By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists'" (6:23), and the Cattle chapter answers that plea with its own verdict on swearing: "See how they will lie about themselves and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them!" (6:24), the very verb of 41:48's first clause in another chapter's sentence. The pairing with this sūrah's forty-eight is exact in its cruelty: the oath is an invocation of the true God to deny the false ones, which is itself the scene's proof that men always knew which god was which — the sworn denial arrives one verse after the partners' failure because the failure is what provokes it, and it fails in turn. The chapter had said the private half long ago — "Rather, you assumed that Allah did not know much of what you used to do" (41:22) — the men who thought nothing was noticed will, on that Day, think the noticed could be sworn away, and the sūrah treats that reflex as data about the human animal, not as an argument worth answering at the bar.

**The Verse at the Chapter's Last Seam**

Forty-eight is the chapter's final sentence about the partners, and its brevity — two clauses where the polemicists of Mecca wrote books against the sanctuary's gods — is the sūrah's answer to the genre: it does not refute the gods, it attends their bankruptcy. From here the chapter leaves the courtroom entirely and turns, in its closing movement, to the one remaining exhibit — the human being's temperament when prosperity and adversity pass over it (41:49) — because the sūrah's last argument is not with the idols but with the psychology that kept calling them: the same "man" who never tires of asking for good and despairs when touched by harm, a creature the next verse will portrait in two sentences. What the chapter has spent forty-seven verses proving about heaven's ledger, it now spends seven proving about the heart's, and the seam is perfect: the partners failed (41:48's two clauses) — now let the reader see what kind of creature chose them, which is where the sūrah's final address begins.

The verb "they will know" (*ʿarafo*) matters more than it looks: this is the knowledge of recognition, the dawning that confirms what the proof-letters said and what the habit denied, the recognition the prisoners' late cry voices elsewhere in this Book (32:12's seeing and hearing), and the verse's own knowledge-theme since forty-seven (the Hour's drawer, the seed's sheath).
verses.49:
> One never tires of praying for good. And if touched with evil, they become desperate and hopeless

**"Praying for Good" — Asking Without a Ceiling**

The good he never stops asking for is, in the old glosses, wealth, health, and their like (IJ, IK, Ṭ), and al-Rāzī adds the psychology the verb requires: no amount satiates him so that he stops asking for more — the prayer has no end condition, and *lā yaṭʿamu* ("he does not sate") makes the asking not an act but a state. The Book gives the same portrait its two coordinates elsewhere: "Indeed, humankind was created impatient: distressed when touched with evil, and withholding when touched with good" (70:19–21), and "humans ˹swiftly˺ pray for evil as they pray for good. For humankind is ever hasty" (17:11) — the second verse's confession being the sūrah's own, that the direction of this tireless asking is unreliable: the same tongue that begs for wealth begs, in anger, for harm.

**"Touched with Evil" — The Theology of Contact**

*Massa* — touch — is the verse's small verb, and it is the chapter's own: the damned of ʿĀd were made to "taste a humiliating punishment" (41:16), the disbelievers will "taste" severe punishment (41:27), mercy will be "tasted" (41:50, next verse), and torment finally "tasted" (41:50's close). The sūrah's metaphysics of experience is contact: good and evil are not arguments but surfaces that meet the skin, and the verse before us names the human as whatever reacts wrongly when the meeting happens. To the touch of evil his response is *qanūṭ* — despairing — a superlative form whose root means to be cut off, the man severed from the expectation of good. The pairing the chapter insists on is that the same organ of reception runs both of his states: the hand that reaches for more and the hand that lets go of everything are one hand, which is why 41:49's two clauses are, in form, a single sentence about touch.

**The Counter-Portrait Nineteen Verses Back**

Set the man of 41:49 next to "those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then stand firm" (41:30), and the sūrah's design becomes visible: the steadfast receive from the angels precisely the two words this man cannot hear — "do not fear, and do not grieve" — a prohibition addressed, in the classical reading, to exactly the twin maladies: fear for what is coming and grief for what is lost. The chapter has built its final section as a mirror of its consolation section: where the allies hear the angels descend and say "do not fear and do not grieve" (41:30), the generic human's organs here oscillate between asking and collapse. The verse is not introducing new material; it is reissuing the chapter's first division — the two classes — in psychological rather than judicial language, so that the reader understands the trial of 41:19–24 and the welcome of 41:30–32 as outcomes of the same question: what do you do when something touches you.

**Why the Chapter Turns to Psychology Last**

The sūrah has defended its book against noise (41:26), distortion (41:40), and denial (41:41), and defended its prophet (41:43) and its language (41:44); having done so, it spends its final paragraphs not on the Meccans' arguments but on the human's temperament, and the placement is the chapter's last word about method. Proof that reaches only the convinced will not reach Mecca; so the sūrah makes its final exhibits the reader's own inconstancy — asking without end, despairing at a touch, presuming upon mercy (41:50), turning away when given (41:51) — and then, as if to answer the despair it has just drawn, promises that signs will keep arriving in the horizons and in the self (41:53). The chapter's ending is thus a treatment, not a threat: it has diagnosed the species so precisely that the final call to certainty is addressed to a patient who recognizes his own chart. Whoever reads 41:49 and sees a description of himself has already been read by it.

The verse's halves are not two personalities but one, and the sūrah's audience should have learned it from the chapter's anatomy of the ear and heart (41:5, 41:26): the tireless asker and the instant despairer are the same creature because both are governed by circumstance rather than conviction — "there are some who worship Allah on the verge ˹of faith˺: if they are blessed with something good, they are content with it; but if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter" (22:11), the Pilgrim chapter's verdict on exactly this weather-vane piety.
verses.50:
> And if We let them taste a mercy from Us after being touched with adversity, they will certainly say, “This is what I deserve. I do not think the Hour will ˹ever˺ come. And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, the finest reward with Him will definitely be mine.” But We will surely inform the disbelievers of what they used to do. And We will certainly make them taste a harsh torment

**"This Is What I Deserve" — Entitlement as Theology**

The exclamation — *hādhihi lī*, "this is mine" — is one of the Quran's small catchwords for the religious instinct of ownership, and the sources read it precisely: the man feels the mercy is owed to him (IJ, IK, R) or that God is pleased with him and so rewarded him (Ṭ). Its most famous sibling is Qārun's — "I have been granted all this only because of ˹my˺ knowledge" (39:49) and in the Story chapter's version, "He replied, 'I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have'" (28:78) — and both scenes are cited in this verse's own margin, because Fuṣṭilat's man completes the theft that Qārun began: he does not merely credit his own knowledge; he converts the gift into property and the property into a forecast of final success. The clause is a miniature of the whole chapter's indictment, since its opening exchange: the men who demanded the recitation be drowned had already assigned themselves the venue, the argument, and now, in this verse, the verdict.

**The Logic Stolen from Verse Forty-Six**

Two verses back the sūrah established that whoever does good has it *for their own selves* (41:46), a rule meant to teach ownership of consequences; verse fifty shows the same ownership grammar mutated into a claim against God — "the deed is mine, therefore the reward is mine, therefore the next reward is mine." The readers' psychology is exact: nothing in the man's sentence mentions God as giver except to make Him a confirmer; the mercy is "tasted" (the verse's own verb, in the chapter's contact-language since 41:16), and the taste is taken as a signature on his own file rather than a gift from another's hand. This is why the chapter placed the ownership clause right before the presumption: the Book's just ledger is the one instrument that can be forged, and verse fifty demonstrates the forgery in real time — a man quoting, in practice, a corrupted copy of 41:46.

**"I Do Not Think the Hour Will Ever Come"**

The middle confession ties his economics to his the doctrine of the Last Day, and the Book knows the type at its full length: the owner of the two gardens says it verbatim in his — "I do not think ˹this˺ will ever perish, nor do I think the Hour will ˹ever˺ come. And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, I will definitely get a far better outcome than ˹all˺ this" (18:35–36) — which is Fuṣṭilat's verse in a longer dress, down to the conditional "if I am returned." The syntax of the doubt is the datum: the Hour is not denied on evidence but *discounted as inference from his own case* — prosperity, to this mind, is a proof that no audit is coming — and the cave chapter shows the same inference collapsing into the loss of both worlds. The Smoke chapter's residents put its end point on record: when told that Allah's promise is true, "you said ˹mockingly˺, 'We do not know what the Hour is! We think it is no more than speculation, and we are not convinced'" (45:32) — the Hour demoted to rumor by men who were enjoying their credit.

**The Conditional That Keeps a God He Does Not Expect**

"And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, the finest reward with Him will definitely be mine" — the verse's most revealing phrase is its *if*: the man cannot bring himself to close the door on the meeting, so he reopens it as a favorable appointment. He will not surrender God, only his accountability; the return is allowed precisely to be a promotion ("the finest reward with Him"), his worldly balance sheet simply carried into the next office. The sūrah has already diagnosed this bargaining instinct — the trade the lost made when they preferred guidance for blindness (41:23's scene, whose ledger 2:16 describes in the Book's standing idiom) — and here the trade is Last-Day: a God who is kept on retainer as guarantor of one's merits.
verses.51:
> When We show favour to someone, they turn away, acting arrogantly. And when touched with evil, they make endless prayers ˹for good˺

**The Double Retreat**

The first clause's Arabic gives the turning two verbs for the price of one — *tawallā* and *nafā bi-janbihi*, turn away and thrust his side aside — the posture of a man rolling his body away from a caller, and the translators' "turn away, acting arrogantly" keeps both motions: refusal of the favor's Giver and self-removal from the room of gratitude. The source-note supplies the engine in one line: human beings turn away and withdraw because they consider themselves beyond need, which is the verse the Prophet of this very sūrah was reciting when the chapter of the Clot had cried: "Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds, once they think they are self-sufficient" (96:6–7). Fuṣṭilat's triptych thus ends where the first-revealed words began: the same self-sufficiency that made the man transgress is what makes him thankless, and the sūrah's psychology closes on the oldest of its diagnoses.

**A Twin Verse in the Isra**

The Night Journey chapter hands this verse's identical twin: "When We grant people Our favours, they turn away, acting arrogantly. But when touched with evil, they lose all hope" (17:83) — the same two-touch structure, favor turning the man away, evil ending his hope, the same verb of touch the sūrah has used since 41:49. The parallel is worth citing for what it changes: there the object is "people" in the plural of history, here the generic singular again, and the second half in Fuṣṭilat replaces despair with *endless prayer* — which is the more damning variant, because the man does not stop praying; he only redirects prayer to circumstance. The reader who compares the twins sees the sūrah's precise point: the type is not the one who has no God in affliction but the one whose God exists only in affliction, and whose relief therefore requires an exit from the presence of the One he just addressed.

**"Endless Prayers" — and the Quarrel About Them**

The final noun — *ḍuʿāʾ ʿarīḍ* — spread the old readers across a genuine range. The disagreement dissolves into the verse's design: either way the man's prayer is measured by its expiry date, and 41:51 exists to stamp it. "Endless" in the first reading means verbose; in the second it means persistent; in both, it means mortal — a prayer that ends when the trouble ends is not worship but negotiation, and the chapter that began with prayer for good that never tires (41:49) now shows the negotiation at its final stage, conducted as though the counterparty were the affliction rather than Allah.

**Who Does What — the Verse's Quiet Grammar Lesson**

Mark the distribution of verbs across the triptych's last line: favor is something *We* actively show ("When We show favor"), while evil is expressed in the passive of touch ("when touched"), and the older readers press the asymmetry into a rule of theology: "˹Say,˺ 'Whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself'" (4:79), the Women chapter's sentence that assigns grammar its ethics. The man of 41:51 does exactly the opposite with the same data: he attributes favor to himself (41:50) and — the verse here completes the portrait — attributes God to the evil, addressing his petitions to the moment of contact while his moments of giving leave him unthanked. The sūrah's two-verb clause is thus a miniature reversal of 4:79's order of gratitude, and the chapter places it after its own ledger verse (41:46) so that ownership, entitlement, and ingratitude stand revealed as one fault in three costumes.

But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried out to Us to remove any hardship" (10:12) — the three postures, the full liturgy of distress, then the clean forgetting, the past tense of his own pleading erased.
verses.52:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if this ˹Quran˺ is ˹truly˺ from Allah and you deny it: who can be more astray than those who have gone too far in opposition ˹to the truth˺?”

**The Last Command of the Long Debate**

The chapter's closing sequence has run from the Hour's sealed drawer (41:47) through the partners' disappearance (41:48) to three verses of human physiology (49–51); now, at the end of the argument, comes the third and last *qul* of this sūrah's final movement — Say: have you considered? (earlier commands of the same form opened the chapter's creed-paragraph with "I am only a man" in 41:6 and the twin announcement of the book's twin offices in 41:44). The imperative marks the transition the whole chapter has engineered: description gives way to address once more, and the address is not a threat but a question, the same mode in which the sūrah has posed every decisive challenge (41:33's "whose words are better?" and 41:40's "who is better?"). Five hundred verses of Qur'anic argument have no stronger ending available than a question the audience must answer against itself, and Fuṣṭilat chooses exactly that.

**The Conditional That Removes the Book**

"Imagine if this is from Allah and you deny it" — the verse's thought-experiment performs, for the whole Quran, the same operation 41:44 performed for its Arabic: there the language was inverted to show the objection was never about language; here the source is inverted to show the denial was never about evidence. Suppose, the verse says, the premise you dispute is true — and see what your denial becomes: not a mistaken conclusion but a condition of soul, measurable without settling the question you came to settle. Rāzī, in the source's summary, reads the whole clause as the sūrah's answer to 41:5's declaration — "Our hearts are veiled against what you are calling us to, there is deafness in our ears, and there is a barrier between us and you. So do ˹whatever you want˺ and so shall we!"" — and the fit is exact: the veil-thesis claims that the disagreement is a matter of insulation, and the conditional replies that even granting their own fear of contact, the position they have taken is not insulation but perdition. The objection of 41:5 is given one last hearing at 41:52, and dismissed by arithmetic rather than thunder.

**"Who Is More Astray?" — the Superlative of Loss**

The interrogative is the sūrah's signature device in its negative form (41:33 asked "whose words are better?" and crowned a class; here the superlative asks "who is more astray?" and finds no one), and the parallel elsewhere sharpens it: "And who could be more astray than those who call upon others besides Allah—˹others˺ that cannot respond to them until the Day of Judgment, and are ˹even˺ unaware of their calls?" (46:5), the Sandhills chapter's version of the same ranking applied to idol-prayer. Fuṣṭilat's ranking is worse because its object is narrower: not a wrong act but a stance toward a specific book, "this" — *hādhā* — the present Quran in the hearers' hands, denied by men who had it before them for years, watched it grow, and could not produce its opposite.

**Why the Chapter Has One Verse Left to Prove**

Structurally, 41:52 is the sūrah's last word addressed to the opponents in the mode of dispute; what follows (41:53–54) is addressed about them, not to them — the promise of showing the signs, and the summing verdict of the Witness — and that order is the chapter's final epistemological statement. A question like this one ("who is more astray?") assumes an audience capable of answering, and after 41:49–51 the sūrah has described why most are not; the remaining two verses therefore switch to divine first person — *We will show them*, *We will inform them* (41:50's verb recurring) — and let history and creation do the convincing that argument left unfinished. This is why 41:52 sits where it does: it is the hinge that turns rhetoric in on itself, questions the questioners once, and then hands the case over to the witnesses every later reader can check. The next verse's promise begins the transfer; this one ends the trial by closing the defendant's brief instead of the judge's.

The Sandhills chapter preserves this verse's closer twin, and the sources print them together: "Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Consider if this ˹Quran˺ is ˹truly˺ from Allah and you deny it, and a witness from the Children of Israel attests to it and then believes, whereas you act arrogantly'" (46:10), where the same conditional is settled on the spot by an insider witness and the charge becomes pride rather than doubt.
verses.53:
> We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth. Is it not enough that your Lord is a Witness over all things

**The Future Tense of Proof**

*Sanurīhim āyātinā* — We will keep showing them — the sūrah's most optimistic verb-form, a first-person plural imperfect with God as its subject and open-ended time as its adverb. Many of the commentators understood the promise at its plainest: the sūrah is saying that the argument will not be left to the hearers' impatience; God answers the question "who can be more astray?" (41:52) by taking over the case-file of proof across history itself.

**The Two Witnesses, and What the First Readers Made of Them**

The horizons and the selves — *al-āfāq wa-l-anfus* — gathered a spectrum of referents that is itself instructive: the conquest of the lands around Mecca (R) or the regions to which Islam spread (IJ, Q, Ṭ); the taking of Mecca itself or the day of Badr as the sign "within" (Q, R, IJ); the destruction of other civilizations and the withholding of rain (Q, IJ); and the bodies' illnesses, the celestial bodies and the alternation of night and day, and the stages of human life from conception through birth to death (Q, R), in the same list the Pilgrim chapter gives when it turns the embryo into evidence (22:5's stages, cited in that chapter's own sign-catalogue). The verse's genius is that it licenses the whole spectrum at once: the promise is not "the next sign will be X" but "the showing will not stop until the seeing is total," and the plural of readers was wise enough to keep every candidate on the list rather than pick one. A verse with a closed referent proves one thing; this one proves by method.

**The Self as Second Laboratory**

That the inner witness is not a metaphor but the same kind of data as the outer is guaranteed by the Book's near-verbatim twin: "There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith, as there are within yourselves. Can you not see?" (51:20–21), the Chapter that scatters the pair into the earth and the soul and closes with the smallest possible imperative, *see*. Fuṣṭilat adds what the scattering chapter lacks — the *until* — making sight a term of proof rather than an offer; and its own earlier verses have already filled the "selves" with forensic content: the organs as witnesses (41:20), the skin's confession (41:21), the ear's disease (41:44). The human being who cannot trust his own anatomy in the trial of 41:19–24 is the same being whose anatomy will now testify to the truth of the book, and the verse's ambition is exactly to close that circle: the courtroom and the laboratory are one body.

**"Until It Becomes Clear That It Is the Truth" — and the Pronoun's Freedom**

The purpose clause hangs on a bare pronoun — *annahu* — and the sources list its candidates without closing the list: the Quran (IJ, Q), the religion of Islam (Q), the whole message the Prophet carries (IJ), his true prophethood (Q), or — with the antecedent supplied as "everything" — the truth of all created things, or God Himself, so that it reads "that He is the Truth." The ambiguity is not a flaw the sūrah failed to repair but an economy it performed: the clause makes every fulfilled sign confirm every candidate, so that conquest, rain, embryology, and the self's own testimony each count as proof of the book and of its Sender at once. And the verb of clarity — *yatabayyana* — is of the same root the chapter has worn since its title (41:3's explained verses, 41:52's veils removed), and here at last it names the end of that process: exposition (tafsīl) exists to produce clarity (bayān) by showing what the veil refused to see. The sūrah's final epistemological word is its first adjective completed.
verses.54:
> They are truly in doubt of the meeting with their Lord! ˹But˺ He is indeed Fully Aware of everything

**"The Meeting with Their Lord" — the Hour Named by Its Verb**

*Liqāʾ* — meeting — is the Hour's gentlest name, and the chapter has prepared it everywhere: the organs' testimony is the meeting's procedure, the angels' descent its courier service, and the skin's speech its transcript; elsewhere the Book names the same state's denial in one clean line: "Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, being pleased and content with this worldly life, and who are heedless of Our signs" (10:7), which is the sūrah's own diagnosis (41:49–51) filed under the meeting's heading. But the word's true echo is inside the chapter, forty-six verses back: the great command to repel evil with what is better closed with "none is *granted* this (*yulaqqā*) except those who are patient" (41:35), and the passive of *l-i-q-y* there — to be made to receive, to be met with a gift — is the same root as the meeting here. Fuṣṭilat's last word about the Hour therefore completes its last word about ethics: the meeting is what the patient were being fitted to receive, and doubt of it is not an intellectual position but a failure of the capacity to be met. The sūrah has said, in its final sentence, that everything it taught was about this.

**"He is Fully Aware of Everything" — the Encompassing as Attribute**

The closing phrase translates *muḥīṭ* — encompassing, encircling, the participle of the root used for a wall that surrounds a garden and for water that closes on a ship — and the sources record the small, consequential argument over what He encompasses us *with*: most read the verse's final attribute as power and knowledge (IK, Q, R), while others press the Quran's own pairing of the verb's objects and conclude that only two attributes are ever said to encompass all things: the angels' prayer, "Our Lord! You encompass everything in ˹Your˺ mercy and knowledge" (40:7), and "Allah certainly encompasses all things in ˹His˺ knowledge" (65:12). Read as the second party reads it, the sūrah's last word rhymes with its first: the chapter that descended from the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful (41:2) closes on an encompassment in mercy and knowledge, and the doubt of the meeting — verse fifty-four's subject — is enclosed from both sides by what the doubler cannot escape and cannot outrun.

**The Enveloped, and the Face That Remains**

The commentators who read the encompassing inwardly push it one step further, and their step is worth the record: al-Kāshānī glosses that nothing escapes His encompassing because nothing has being, reality, or self apart from what His knowledge and His being give it — an argument the sources anchor in the Quran's own annihilation-verses: "Everything is bound to perish except He Himself" (28:88), and "Every being on earth is bound to perish. Only your Lord Himself, full of Majesty and Honour, will remain forever" (55:26–27). The reader should weigh this as the chapter's inner dimension, not as its last word — but it is a fitting last word to weigh, because a sūrah that has described a doubt (41:54's first clause) in a book (41:41–42), before a court (41:19–24), under a sky (41:9–12), arrives finally at the sentence that leaves nothing outside: the doubting, the book, the court, and the sky are all inside the encompassment, and only the Encompasser remains. The chapter's restraint in the end is its doctrine: it says awareness, not verdict, because at the end there is no verdict that is not already contained in it. Fuṣṭilat's structure now closes visibly: its first verses told the audience that the book was explained for people who know (41:3) and that denial was a choice made after hearing (41:4–5); its last verses tell them that denial is a doubt about the meeting, and that the One they doubt is aware of everything — the ring is exact because the whole sūrah has been one long answer to the sentence "our hearts are veiled against what you are calling us to" (41:5).
